title: Kenyan Swahili vs Sanifu
summary: Why this app teaches the Swahili people actually speak in Nairobi — and where the "Sanifu" look-ups come in.

blocks.text: **Sanifu** ("standard") is the Swahili of textbooks, Tanzanian schools and the news. **Kenyan Swahili** is what you hear on the matatu, at the kibanda and in the office: the same language, but faster, more relaxed, and simplified in a few predictable ways.

The biggest simplification is in **noun classes**. Sanifu has around 15 of them, each with its own agreement. Everyday Kenyan speech leans on just two: **m/wa** for people and animals, and **n/n** for nearly everything else. That's why you'll hear *gari yangu* (my car) and *kitabu hii* (this book) in Nairobi, where Sanifu says *gari langu* and *kitabu hiki*.

blocks.caption: The same sentence, two registers
rows: Kiti ya mbele iko na mtu.

blocks.text: Kabisa teaches the **Kenyan form first** and shows the Sanifu form as a "good to know" look-up. Look for **Sanifu** in the word tooltips and vocabulary lists.

Both are understood everywhere in Kenya. Sanifu sounds educated and a bit formal; Kenyan sounds natural and friendly. If you aim to be understood on the street — not to pass a Tanzanian exam — Kenyan first is the right call.

examples.note: Kenyan — Sanifu would say Sijambo / Niko salama.

title: Greetings: Mambo, Habari, Hujambo
summary: Who you greet decides how you greet. Casual, polite and traditional greetings — and the right answer to each.

blocks.text: In Kenya you always greet before anything else. There are three families of greetings, and each has a fixed answer:
Every "Habari…?" is answered with **Nzuri** — even on a terrible day. The real news comes *after* the greeting.
To several people, the casual greetings switch to plural: **Mko aje?** → **Tuko poa.** Traditional: **Hamjambo?** → **Hatujambo.**
Goodbyes: **Kwa heri** (one person), **Kwaherini** (several), **Tuonane baadaye** (see you later), **Tutaonana** (see you).
"Jambo!" is mostly said to tourists. Kenyans rarely use it with each other — try "Mambo?" or "Habari?" instead.

examples.english: How are you all? — We're fine.

title: Subject Prefixes: ni-, u-, a-, tu-, m-, wa-
summary: Every Swahili verb starts with a prefix that tells you WHO is doing it.

blocks.text: Swahili verbs are built like Lego. The first brick is the **subject prefix** — it does the job of English "I, you, he…". You often don't need the separate pronoun (mimi, wewe…) at all: *Ninaenda* already means "I am going".
There is no "he" vs "she" in Swahili — **a-** covers both. Context does the work.
The pronouns (mimi, wewe, yeye…) are used for emphasis or contrast: *Mimi ninaenda, wewe unabaki* — **I**'m going, **you**'re staying.

examples.note: i- because bei is an n/n noun.

title: Present Tense -na-
summary: Subject + -na- + verb = what's happening now (or generally). Kenyans often squeeze ni-na- into na-.

blocks.text: The present tense formula is: **subject prefix + -na- + verb stem**.
It covers both "I am going" and "I go": *Ninafanya kazi Safaricom* = I work at Safaricom.
**Kenyan shortcut:** ni-na- becomes **na-** in everyday speech: *naenda, nataka, naomba, naelewa*. You'll hear this far more than the full form.
Short verbs like **kula** (eat), **kunywa** (drink) and **kuja** (come) keep their **ku-**: *ninakula, unakunywa, anakuja*.
Sanifu uses **kwenda** for "to go" (ninakwenda); Kenyans say **kuenda** (ninaenda / naenda).

title: -ko: Being Somewhere (Niko, Uko, Iko)
summary: -ko means "be at a place" — and in Kenya, also "how you're doing" (Niko poa).

blocks.text: Use **-ko** for where someone or something is. It takes the subject prefix directly — no tense marker.
**Location:** *Uko wapi?* — Where are you? *Niko Westlands Mall.* — I'm at Westlands Mall. *Stage iko wapi?* — Where is the stage?
**How you are:** *Uko aje? — Niko poa.* (How are you? — I'm fine.)
Kenyans also use **-ko na** for "have": *Uko na pesa?* (Do you have money?) — Sanifu prefers *Una pesa?*
Kenyans often shorten yuko to **ako**: *Ako wapi?* (Where is he?). Sanifu: *Yuko wapi?*

title: Ni and Si: "Is" and "Is Not"
summary: Ni (is, am, are) never changes. Si is its negative. Use -ko for location instead.

blocks.text: **Ni** links two things: *Mimi ni John* (I am John), *Hii ni chai* (this is tea). It's the same for every person and every number.
**Si** is the negative: *Si mbali* (it's not far), *Mimi si dereva* (I'm not the driver). Kenyans often say **sio**: *Sio mbali*.

blocks.caption: Ni vs -ko vs -na
rows: Yeye ni mwalimu. — She is a teacher.
Yuko shuleni. — She is at school.
Ana gari. — She has a car.

blocks.text: **Si …?** at the start of a sentence makes a friendly suggestion: *Si tukutane kesho?* — Why don't we meet tomorrow?
**Ndiyo / ndio** works like an emphatic "it is": *Ndiyo hii* — this is the one / here it is.

title: Question Words: Wapi, Nini, Nani, Gani…
summary: Swahili question words usually go at the END of the sentence — right where the answer would be.

blocks.text: Word order stays the same as a statement: *Unaenda Westlands* (you're going to Westlands) → *Unaenda wapi?* (you're going where?).
**Je, …?** at the start turns any statement into a yes/no question: *Je, una chenji?* — Do you have change? In speech, rising intonation alone does the same.
Ngapi agrees with the noun in Sanifu (*watu wangapi, miti mingapi*). Kenyans mostly use plain **ngapi** for everything except people (wangapi).

title: Our Two Noun Classes: m/wa and n/n
summary: Swahili nouns come in classes that control agreement. Kabisa uses two as the standard: m/wa (people) and n/n (things).

blocks.text: Every Swahili noun belongs to a **class**, and the class decides the prefixes on verbs, adjectives and possessives that go with it. Sanifu has many classes — but Kenyan everyday speech runs on two:

blocks.caption: n/n — things (same word for one and many)

blocks.text: Animals are nouns of many shapes (simba, mbwa, kiboko) but **always take m/wa agreement** because they're living: *simba anakula*, *mbwa wangu*.
**The Kenyan rule of thumb:** if it's a person or animal → m/wa. Anything else → treat it as n/n (i-/zi-, yangu/zangu, hii/hizi). You'll be understood everywhere.
Nouns like **kitabu, gari, mti, ukuta** belong to other classes in Sanifu (ki/vi, ji/ma, m/mi, u/n). Tap a word's **Sanifu** note to see its standard agreement — or open "Other Noun Classes".

title: Negative Present: si- … -i
summary: To say "I don't…", swap the subject prefix for its negative, drop -na-, and change the final -a to -i.

blocks.text: Three changes turn *ninataka* (I want) into *sitaki* (I don't want):

items: Use the **negative subject prefix** (si-, hu-, ha-…)

blocks.text: Verbs that don't end in -a (borrowed from Arabic) keep their ending: *sifikiri* (I don't think), *sijali* (I don't care).
The three you'll use every day: **Sijui** (I don't know), **Sielewi** (I don't understand), **Sitaki** (I don't want).

title: Nina / Sina: Having (and "There Is")
summary: Swahili "have" is literally "be with": ni- + -na. Kuna = there is; hakuna = there isn't.

blocks.text: **Kuna** = there is / there are (lit. "the place has"): *Kuna magari mingi* — there's traffic. **Hakuna** = there isn't: *Hakuna shida* — no problem.
In other tenses, use **kuwa na** (to be with): *nilikuwa na* (I had), *nitakuwa na* (I will have), *ningekuwa na* (if I had).
Kenyans often say **-ko na** instead: *Uko na chenji?* (Do you have change?), *Ako na gari* (She has a car). Sanifu: *Una chenji? Ana gari.*
**Haina shida / Hakuna shida / Hamna shida** — all "no problem". You'll hear them a hundred times a day.

title: Possessives: Wangu, Yangu, Zangu
summary: my, your, his… = -angu, -ako, -ake, -etu, -enu, -ao, with a prefix that agrees with the THING owned.

blocks.text: The ending tells you **who owns** it; the first letter agrees with **what is owned**.
*Mtoto wangu* (my child), *watoto wangu* (my children), *nyumba yangu* (my house), *nyumba zangu* (my houses).

**Family words** (mama, baba, dada, kaka, nyanya) take the n/n form even though they're people: *mama yangu, dada yake*. And Kenyans use **yangu** for most things: *jina yangu, gari yangu, simu yangu*.
Contractions are everywhere: **mamangu** (my mum), **babako** (your dad), **dadake** (his/her sister), **mwenzangu** (my colleague). And **kwangu / kwako / kwetu** = my place / your place / our home.
**Of** works the same way: *mtoto wa Kamau* (m/wa), *nyumba ya Kamau* (n/n), *habari za asubuhi* (n/n plural).
Sanifu: *jina **langu***, *gari **langu*** (ji/ma), *kitabu **changu*** (ki/vi), *mti **wangu*** (m/mi). See "Other Noun Classes".

title: This & That: Huyu, Hii, Yule, Ile
summary: Three distances (here / near you / over there), agreeing with m/wa or n/n.

blocks.text: They usually come **after** the noun: *mtu huyu* (this person), *nyumba ile* (that house). Before the noun they add emphasis: *huyu mtu* — THIS guy.
**Hii hapa / Hizi hapa** = here it is / here they are (handing something over).
**Hii** is Kenya's all-purpose "this": *gari hii, kitabu hii, chakula hii*. Sanifu would say gari hili, kitabu hiki, chakula hiki.
Other Sanifu forms: ki/vi **hiki / hivi**, ji/ma **hili / haya**, m/mi **huu / hii**, u **huu**.

title: Numbers & Money
summary: Counting, prices, and Nairobi money slang (bob, punch, thao).

blocks.text: Numbers join with **na**: 250 = *mia mbili na hamsini*; 1,500 = *elfu moja mia tano*.
**People** take wa- numbers: *watoto wawili* (two children). **Things** (n/n) use the plain form: *nyumba mbili, chapati tatu*.
Market slang: **bob** = shillings (mia tano bob), **punch** = 500, **thao** = 1,000. Asking prices: **Bei gani?** / **Ni pesa ngapi?** / **Ngapi?**
In Sanifu, numbers agree with every class: *viti viwili* (ki/vi), *miti miwili* (m/mi), *magari mawili* (ji/ma).

title: Other Noun Classes (Sanifu Look-up)
summary: A reference for the classes Kenyans mostly flatten into n/n: ki/vi, ji/ma, m/mi, u/n and the place classes.

blocks.text: Kabisa uses m/wa and n/n everywhere. This page is your **look-up** for when you meet a Sanifu form — on the news, in a book, or from a teacher.

Some Sanifu agreements survive in Kenyan speech for very common words: **maji mengi** (lots of water), **matokeo yatakuja** (results will come), **vidonge viwili** (two tablets), **mtaa wetu** (our neighbourhood).
Tap any word marked **Sanifu** in a lesson to see its standard class and agreement.

examples.english: My book is on the table.
examples.note: Sanifu ki/vi. Kenyan: kitabu yangu iko kwa meza.
Sanifu ji/ma. Kenyan: gari yangu imeharibika.
Sanifu m/mi. Kenyan: mti hii ni ndefu.

title: Future Tense -ta-
summary: Swap -na- for -ta- and you're in the future. Negative: si-ta-, hu-ta-, ha-ta-…

blocks.text: The negative future keeps **-ta-** and the final **-a**: *sitaenda* (I won't go).
Short verbs keep **ku-**: *nitakula* (I'll eat), *utakuja?* (will you come?), *nitakunywa* (I'll drink).
Kenyans often use the plain present for planned future: *Kesho naenda Naivasha* — Tomorrow I'm going to Naivasha.
**Nitakuwa** = I will be: *Nitakuwa tayari* (I'll be ready), *Nitakuwa na pesa* (I'll have money).

title: Commands: Panda! Shuka! Njoo!
summary: The bare verb stem is a command. Add -eni for several people. Use usi-…-e for "don't".

blocks.text: To include **me / him / them**, use the object prefix and end in **-e**: *Nipe!* (give me), *Niletee chai* (bring me tea), *Mwambie* (tell him).
A bare command is normal in a matatu or at a stall. For more politeness add **tafadhali** or use the subjunctive: *Uniletee chai, tafadhali* — see "Polite Requests".

title: Helper Verbs: Weza, Taka, Lazima, Inabidi
summary: Can, want to, must, have to — followed by an infinitive (ku-) or a subjunctive.

blocks.caption: Pattern
rows: Naweza kupata chai? — Can I get tea?
Nataka kulala. — I want to sleep.
Inabidi niende. — I have to go.

blocks.text: Negatives: *siwezi* (I can't), *hawezi* (he can't), *sitaki kuenda* (I don't want to go), *si lazima* (it's not necessary).
**Naweza…?** is the easiest polite way to ask for anything: *Naweza kulipa kwa M-Pesa?* — Can I pay with M-Pesa?

title: The Infinitive: ku- and kuto-
summary: ku- + stem = "to …" (and "…-ing" as a noun). kuto- = "not to".

blocks.text: Dictionary forms start with **ku-**: *kuenda* (to go), *kula* (to eat), *kufanya* (to do). The infinitive also works as a noun: *Kusoma ni muhimu* — Reading is important.
Object prefixes go between ku- and the stem: *kunisaidia* (to help me), *kukuona* (to see you), *kumsalimia* (to greet him).
**kuto-** makes it negative: *kutoelewa* (not understanding / misunderstanding), *kutokuwa na pesa* (not having money).
After **kwa** it means "for …-ing": *Asante kwa kunisaidia* — Thanks for helping me.

examples.english: Thanks for keeping it for me.
Not having money is no shame.

title: Telling Time: Swahili Hours
summary: The Swahili day starts at sunrise: 7 a.m. is saa moja ("the first hour"). Add or subtract six.

blocks.text: Add **asubuhi** (morning), **mchana** (afternoon), **jioni** (evening) or **usiku** (night) to be clear.
Trick: clock time ± 6. 10 a.m. → 10 − 6 = **saa nne**. And always check whether someone means Swahili or English time — Kenyans switch freely ("saa moja" vs "seven").
**Saa ngapi?** = What time? **Saa moja** can also mean "one hour" — context tells you.

examples.swahili: Saa kumi na mbili na nusu.

title: Places: -ni, Kwenye, Kwa
summary: Three ways to say at / in / to a place: the -ni suffix, kwenye, and the very Kenyan kwa.

blocks.text: **-ni** on a noun = at / in / to it: *soko → sokoni* (at the market), *kazi → kazini* (at work), *nyumba → nyumbani* (at home), *jiko → jikoni* (in the kitchen).
**Kwenye** = at / on / in (very flexible): *kwenye meza* (on the table), *kwenye orodha* (on the list), *kwenye kona* (at the corner).
**Kwa** = at someone's place, by, with: *kwa Kevin* (at Kevin's), *kwa M-Pesa* (by M-Pesa), *kwa miguu* (on foot). **Kwangu / kwako / kwetu** = my place / your place / our home.
Kenyans use **kwa** where Sanifu prefers -ni or kwenye: *till iko kwa ukuta* (Sanifu: ukutani), *kwa kona ya kwanza* (Sanifu: kwenye kona ya kwanza).
Names of countries and cities never take -ni: *Ninaenda Nairobi*, *Nitaenda Marekani*.

examples.english: Put the dishes in the sink.

title: Past Tense -li-
summary: Subject + -li- + verb = something that happened. Short verbs keep ku-.

blocks.text: Short verbs keep **ku-**: *nilikula* (I ate), *alikuja* (she came), *tulikunywa* (we drank).
**Nilikuwa** = I was. **Kulikuwa na** = there was / there were.
In a story, after the first -li- verb, Swahili often switches to **-ka-** for "and then…": *Nilifika, nikakutafuta* — I arrived and (then) looked for you. See "-ki-, -po-, -ka-".

title: Negative Past: si-ku-
summary: Negative subject + -ku- + verb (ending stays -a) = "didn't".

blocks.text: Unlike the present negative, the final **-a stays**: *sikuenda* (I didn't go), not *sikuendi*.
Careful: **sioni** = I don't see (now), **sikuona** = I didn't see, **sijaona** = I haven't seen (yet).
With short verbs, Sanifu says *sikula* (I didn't eat); many Kenyans say *sikukula*. Both are understood.

examples.english: You didn't pick up the phone.

title: Object Infixes: -ni-, -ku-, -m-, -wa-
summary: Me, you, him, them — tucked inside the verb, right before the stem.

blocks.text: Swahili puts the object **inside** the verb: subject + tense + **object** + stem. *Ni-li-**ku**-ona* = I saw **you**.
Use **-mw-** before a vowel: *mwambie* (tell him), *nilimwona* (I saw him).
With people, the object marker is almost always used, even when the person is named: *Nilimwona **Baraka*** — I saw Baraka.
Commands with an object end in **-e**: *Nipe* (give me), *Mwambie* (tell him), *Niletee* (bring me).

title: Perfect -me-: Has Done / Is Now
summary: -me- = something has happened and still matters now. With some verbs it describes a state: nimechoka = I'm tired.

blocks.text: Some verbs describe a **state** in -me-, so English uses "is / am":

blocks.caption: State verbs
rows: long time no see! / you're lost

blocks.text: **Umepotea!** (lit. "you've got lost") is how Kenyans say "long time no see!"
Short verbs keep ku-: *umekula?* (have you eaten?), *amekuja* (she's come).

title: Not Yet: -ja- and Bado
summary: Negative subject + -ja- + verb = hasn't (yet). Often with bado.

blocks.text: **Bado** = still / (not) yet. *Bado hajafika* = She hasn't arrived yet. On its own, *Bado!* = Not yet!
Short verbs: *sijala* (I haven't eaten — Kenyans also say *sijakula*), *hajaja* (he hasn't come).
Answer a -me- question with -ja-: *Umekula? — Bado sijala.* (Have you eaten? — Not yet.)

title: -wahi: Ever and Never
summary: -wahi + infinitive = "ever". Sijawahi kuona = I've never seen.

blocks.text: On its own, **kuwahi** means "to be on time / make it": *Leo nimewahi!* — Today I made it on time!
As a helper verb before an infinitive, it means **ever**:

blocks.caption: -wahi + ku-verb
rows: Have you ever seen a lion?
You'll never build a house like this.

blocks.text: **Sijawahi** (I've never) is one of the most useful words for a newcomer: *Sijawahi kula mutura!* — I've never eaten mutura!

examples.english: Have you ever been to Mombasa?
She has worked in Kampala before.

title: Adjectives Agree: Mzuri, Wazuri, Nzuri
summary: Adjectives come after the noun and take its class prefix: m- / wa- for people, n/n form for things.

blocks.text: *Mtu mrefu* (a tall person), *watu warefu* (tall people), *barabara ndefu* (a long road).
Some adjectives never change: **safi** (clean), **rahisi** (cheap/easy), **ghali** (expensive), **tamu** (sweet), **bora** (best).
For things, Kenyans default to the n/n form: *chakula nzuri*, *kitu nzuri*, *gari kubwa*. Sanifu would say chakula kizuri, kitu kizuri, gari kubwa (ji/ma).
Sanifu: ki/vi **kizuri / vizuri**, ji/ma **zuri / mazuri**, m/mi **mzuri / mizuri**.

examples.english: Many of the staff are new.

title: Comparing: Kuliko, Zaidi, Bora
summary: There's no "-er" or "-est" in Swahili: you say "big than" (kubwa kuliko) and "big more" (kubwa zaidi).

blocks.text: **Afadhali** / **heri** = it's better (to…): *Afadhali kuchelewa kuliko kukosa* — Better late than never.
Use **kuliko wote** for people (the tallest of all), **kuliko zote** for n/n things.

examples.swahili: Kikapu hii ni kubwa kuliko ile.
examples.english: This basket is bigger than that one.
Is the fish tastier than the chicken?
Tea is more important than meetings!

title: The Subjunctive: -e for "Let / Should / So That"
summary: Change the final -a to -e (no tense marker) for suggestions, polite requests, wishes and after ili / lazima.

blocks.text: Formula: **subject + (object) + stem with final -e**. No -na-, -li- or -ta-.

blocks.caption: kuenda → -ende
rows: let me go / should I go?
let him go / he should go

blocks.text: Where it's used:

items: **Offers:** *Nikulipe?* (shall I pay you?), *Nikupe chai?* (shall I give you tea?)
**After ili (so that):** *ili nione* (so that I can see)
**After lazima / inabidi / afadhali:** *Lazima tuondoke* (we must leave)

blocks.text: Verbs not ending in -a don't change: *tusubiri* (let's wait), *usisahau* (don't forget), *ujibu* (answer).

title: Polite Requests: Naomba, Uniletee, Ebu
summary: From blunt to gracious: Lete → Niletee → Uniletee → Naomba uniletee.

blocks.caption: The politeness ladder
rows: Bring me tea. (normal at a kibanda)
Would you bring me tea, please. (polite)
May I ask you to bring me tea. (very polite)
Can I get some tea? (polite, easy)

blocks.text: **Naomba** (lit. "I ask / beg") is the gold standard: *Naomba maji* (may I have water), *Naomba leseni yako* (may I see your licence — what a police officer says).
**Ebu / Hebu** softens anything: *Ebu nione* (let me see), *Ebu twende* (come on, let's go).
**Tafadhali** (please) is fine, but Kenyans more often use the subjunctive or naomba. Overusing tafadhali can sound stiff.

examples.english: Please put in three thousand's worth.

title: Verb Extensions: -ia, -wa, -isha, -ana, -ika
summary: One root, many meanings: add a suffix before the final -a to get "for", "be …-ed", "make", "each other" and "get …-ed".

blocks.caption: The five big extensions
rows: leta → letea: bring FOR (niletee = bring me)

blocks.caption: One verb, five ways: kufanya (do)
rows: do for (Nitakufanyia = I'll do it for you)
have done to you (Gari ilifanyiwa ukaguzi)

blocks.text: Vowel harmony: stems with **a, i, u** take -ia / -isha; stems with **e, o** take -ea / -esha: *pika → pikia*, *soma → somea*, *chelewa → chelewesha*.
Watch the meaning shift: **tuma** = send (someone), **tumia** = send to / use. *Nitakutumia* = I'll send (it) to you, but *Nitakutuma* = I'll send YOU (on an errand)!
Passives often take **na** for "by": *Ripoti iliandikwa na Faith* — The report was written by Faith.

title: Talking Like a Kenyan: Kumbe, Basi, Yaani, Si…?
summary: Small words that make you sound natural: surprise, rephrasing, wrapping up, and gentle suggestions.

blocks.caption: Particles
rows: surprise: "oh, so…!" (what you assumed wasn't true)
Kumbe unajua Kiswahili! — Oh, so you speak Swahili!
Basi, twende. — Well then, let's go.
Si tukutane kesho? — Why don't we meet tomorrow?

blocks.text: **Kumbe** is one of the most Kenyan words there is. Use it when you discover something unexpected — it shows you're listening.

examples.english: Well then, today I'll let you go.
Why don't we go have tea?

title: If… Would…: -nge- and -ngali-
summary: -nge- = would / if (present & hypothetical). -ngali- = would have (past). Kenyans use -nge- for both.

blocks.text: Put **-nge-** in BOTH halves: *Ningekuwa na gari, ningenunua kilo kumi* — If I had a car, I'd buy ten kilos.
**-ngali-** is the Sanifu past conditional: *Ningalijua, ningalikuja mapema* — If I had known, I would have come earlier.
**Kenyan habit:** -nge- for the past too, often with **kama** (if) and a time word: *Kama ungemleta fundi mapema, hii haingetokea* — If you had brought the fundi earlier, this wouldn't have happened.
**Ningependa** (I would like) is the polite way to want something: *Ningependa kujua…* — I'd like to know…

examples.english: If I'd known, I'd have come earlier.

examples.swahili: Kama angetimiza ahadi yake, barabara ingekuwa nzuri.
examples.english: If he had kept his promise, the road would be good.

title: -ki- (if), -po- (when), -ka- (and then)
summary: Three little markers for stories and plans: -ki- = if/when (likely), -po- = when (that time), -ka- = and then.

blocks.caption: The trio
rows: Ukifika, nipigie. — When you arrive, call me.
Nilipofika, nilikutafuta. — When I arrived, I looked for you.
Nilifika, nikakutafuta. — I arrived and (then) looked for you.

blocks.text: **-ki- negative:** use **-si-po-**: *Usipoziba ufa, utajenga ukuta* — If you don't fill the crack, you'll build a wall.
**-po- in the future** needs **-ka-**: *atakapofika* — when he arrives.
**-ki-** also means "…-ing" after a past kuwa: *Nilikuwa nikisoma* — I was reading. See "Continuous Tenses".
Short verbs drop ku- with -ki-: *nikija* (if I come), *akila* (if he eats).

examples.english: If you buy three kilos, I'll lower the price for you.
When it started raining, water came in.

title: Who / Which: Amba-, -ye-, Mwenye
summary: Three ways to say "the person who…": ambaye (easy), -ye- inside the verb (elegant), mwenye (Kenyan & handy).

blocks.caption: amba- + reference
rows: mama ambaye huuza mboga — the lady who sells vegetables
watu ambao walikuja — the people who came
dawa ambayo nilipewa — the medicine I was given
nyanya ambazo nilinunua — the tomatoes I bought

blocks.text: **Inside the verb**, after -na-, -li- or -taka-: *a-na-**ye**-enda* (the one who goes), *wa-li-**o**-kuja* (those who came), *i-li-**yo**-anguka* (the one [thing] that fell). Negative: *a-si-**ye**-kubali* (the one who doesn't accept).

**Mwenye / wenye / yenye** = "having / with": *yule mwenye kofia* (the one with the hat), *maembe yenye sukari* (sweet mangoes). Kenyans also use **mwenye** as "who": *mtu mwenye alikuja* — the person who came.
Kenyans prefer **amba-** because it keeps the tense in the main verb and is easy to build. The -ye- forms sound polished — great for proverbs: *Asiyekubali kushindwa si mshindani.*
Sanifu has amba- forms for every class: ambacho, ambavyo (ki/vi), ambalo, ambayo (ji/ma), ambao, ambayo (m/mi), ambapo / ambako (place).

examples.english: The fundi you brought didn't fix it properly.
Did the lady who sold to you give you a good price?

title: Habits: hu- and Kenyan -nga
summary: hu- = usually (Sanifu, any person). Kenyans also add -nga — borrowed from Luhya — to any tense.

blocks.text: **hu-** replaces both the subject prefix and the tense: *Mimi hununua hapa* (I usually buy here), *Wao hufika jioni* (they usually arrive in the evening). Because it doesn't show the person, add a pronoun or noun.
**Huwa** + present = "usually …": *Huwa unakunywa maji ya kutosha?* — Do you usually drink enough water? Very common in Kenya.

blocks.caption: Kenyan -nga
rows: I go to Nyeri every month.

blocks.text: **-nga** came from Luhya and works with any tense — unlike hu-, which is present only. In the negative it becomes **-ngi**: *simfunzangi*.
Proverbs love hu-: *Haba na haba hujaza kibaba* — little by little fills the measure.
Sanifu uses only hu-. -nga is informal Kenyan — friendly, but avoid it in formal writing.

examples.english: Guests usually arrive in the evening.
I usually don't drink much water.

title: Continuous Tenses: Was / Have Been / Will Be …-ing
summary: kuwa in the past, perfect or future + a -ki- (or -na-) verb = an ongoing action.

blocks.caption: Building them
rows: Nilikuwa nikisoma. / Nilikuwa nasoma. — I was reading.
Nimekuwa nikingoja tangu Novemba. — I've been waiting since November.
Nitakuwa nikifanya kazi. — I'll be working.

blocks.text: Both parts take the subject: *Tu**me**kuwa **tu**kisubiri* — We've been waiting. *Wa**li**kuwa **wa**kicheza* — They were playing.
With **-po-**: *Nilipokuwa nikisoma chuo kikuu…* — When I was studying at university…
In everyday Kenyan speech, the second verb is often just present: *Nilikuwa naenda kwa kasi* — I was going fast. Both are correct.

examples.english: We've been waiting for a whole hour.

title: Linking Ideas: Kwamba, Ingawa, Badala ya…
summary: The connectors that turn sentences into stories, arguments and reported speech.

blocks.caption: Connectors
rows: Nimechelewa kwa sababu kuna magari mingi.

blocks.text: **Reported speech:** keep the original tense after kwamba: *Aliniambia kwamba **atakuja*** — He told me that he **would** come (lit. "will come").
Kenyans often drop kwamba in speech, or use **vile**: *Aliniambia atakuja.*

examples.english: You told me that the food would come.

examples.swahili: Ingawa tunaelewa, hata hivyo tuna njaa.
examples.english: Although we understand, we're still hungry.
Instead of chicken, you've brought goat.

title: -vyo-: "The Way" / "As"
summary: Tuck -vyo- into a verb to mean "the way / how / as": unavyotaka = the way you want.

blocks.text: Formula: **subject + tense + -vyo- + verb**. It turns a verb into "the way (that)…".

blocks.caption: Examples
rows: the way you want / as you like
the way he said / as he said

blocks.text: Kenyans also use **vile** + normal verb: *Fanya vile unataka* = Fanya unavyotaka (do as you like).
**Ninavyoona…** (the way I see it…) is a perfect opener for giving your opinion politely.

examples.english: Do the work as best you can.
The way I see it, a good leader listens.

title: Methali & Idioms
summary: Proverbs and idioms that Kenyans actually use — and when to drop them into conversation.

blocks.text: **Methali** (proverbs) are everywhere in Kenya: in speeches, on matatu stickers, and in everyday arguments. Using one at the right moment shows real fluency.

blocks.caption: Methali
rows: The patient one eats ripe fruit.
Good things come to those who wait.
One finger can't crush a louse.
Little by little fills the measure.
If you don't fill the crack, you'll build a wall.
A stitch in time saves nine.
Who wants what's under the bed must bend.
A distant stick doesn't kill a snake.
Who won't accept defeat is no competitor.
Guest, come, so the host may prosper.

blocks.caption: Idioms (nahau) & Kenyan expressions
rows: You left me at the traffic lights.
Time has shown us the back of its head.
Let him miss and be laughed at!
Mambo ni mengi, muda ni mchache.
Things are many, time is little.
So much to do, so little time.

blocks.text: Proverbs use classic grammar: hu- habits (hula, hujaza), -ki- conditions (yakimwagika), -ye- relatives (asiyekubali) and subjunctives (ufike, apone). Tap each word in a lesson to see how it's built.

examples.english: One finger can't crush a louse.
